Yes. A useful way to place them together is to ask not **which voice is the real you**, but **what relation connects different ways of being you**.

In Chapter 5, “Advice from a Caterpillar,” Alice is pressed to give a fixed account of herself. She answers:

“I—I hardly know, sir, just at present—at least I know
who I _was_ when I got up this morning, but I think I must have been
changed several times since then.”

She cannot explain herself because she feels she is no longer unchanged. The scene makes identity a problem of continuity through change, rather than a single description that remains constant.

Hume’s *Of personal identity* gives that problem a philosophical form: when he looks inward, he finds successive perceptions rather than one unchanging self, and argues that we commonly treat related, changing perceptions as one continuing identity. ([Hume, *Of personal identity*, T 1.4.6](https://davidhume.org/texts/t/1/4/6))

Your meeting-and-dinner note offers a concrete version of that tension: you led and spoke quickly in one setting, listened and spoke softly in the other, yet held the same view about the timetable in both. That does not prove that the view is your deepest self, but it does suggest a distinction between **continuity of judgment** and **variation in voice, role, and attention**.

So the contrast might not mean that one voice is authentic and the other false. It may be more productive to ask: **What remains continuous when the way you participate changes—and what becomes possible because it changes?**

silence: at last the Caterpillar took the hookah out of its mouth, and
addressed her in a languid, sleepy voice.

changed several times since then.”

yourself!”

not myself, you see.”

“I don’t see,” said the Caterpillar.

different sizes in a day is very confusing.”

“It isn’t,” said the Caterpillar.

have to turn into a chrysalis—you will some day, you know—and then
after that into a butterfly, I should think you’ll feel it a little
queer, won’t you?”

“Not a bit,” said the Caterpillar.

“Well, perhaps your feelings may be different,” said Alice; “all I know
is, it would feel very queer to _me_.”

“You!” said the Caterpillar contemptuously. “Who are _you?_”

short remarks, and she drew herself up and said, very gravely, “I
think, you ought to tell me who _you_ are, first.”

good reason, and as the Caterpillar seemed to be in a _very_ unpleasant
state of mind, she turned away.

important to say!”

This question 'tis impossible to answer without a manifest contradiction and absurdity; and yet 'tis a question, which must necessarily be answer'd, if we wou'd have the idea of self pass for clear and intelligible. If any impression gives rise to the idea of self, that impression must continue invariably the same, thro' the whole course of our lives; since self is suppos'd to exist after that manner. But there is no impression constant and invariable. Pain | and pleasure, grief and joy, passions and sensations succeed each other, and never all exist at the same time. All these are different, and distinguishable, and separable from each other, and may be separately consider'd, and may exist separately, and have no need of any thing to support their existence. After what manner, therefore, do they belong to self; and how are they connected with it? I never can catch myself at any time without a perception, and never can observe any thing but the perception. When my perceptions are remov'd for any time, as by sound sleep; so long am I insensible of myself, and may truly be said not to exist. And were all my perceptions remov'd by death, and cou'd I neither think, nor feel, nor see, nor love, nor hate after the dissolution of my body, I shou'd be entirely annihilated, nor do I conceive what is farther requisite to make me a perfect non-entity. No—those different voices do not, by themselves, show that your confident self at work is an act or that your quieter family self is the “real” one.

In Chapter 5, *Advice from a Caterpillar*, Alice struggles to give one fixed account of herself:

“I—I hardly know, sir, just at present—at least I know
who I _was_ when I got up this morning, but I think I must have been
changed several times since then.”

Her difficulty is not simply that one version is false; it is that change makes a single, stable description hard to sustain.

Your earlier note gives the contrast a concrete shape: you spoke quickly and led the meeting, listened more at dinner, and still held the same view about the timetable in both settings. That suggests continuity in your judgment even though your manner changed. Feeling comfortable in both settings also matters: it leaves open the possibility that both voices are genuinely yours, each responsive to a different relationship and situation.

Hume’s *Of personal identity* pushes in a related direction: he argues that what we call the self is not one unchanging impression but a succession of changing perceptions connected in experience ([Hume, “Of personal identity”](https://davidhume.org/texts/t/1/4/6)). Neither Hume nor Carroll proves that your two voices are equally authentic, but they both challenge the demand that authenticity must sound the same everywhere.

A useful question may be less “Which voice is the real me?” and more: **What commitments, values, or ways of relating remain recognizable across both voices—and where, if anywhere, do you feel a tension between them?**

Her difficulty is not simply that one version is false; it is that change makes a single, stable description hard to sustain.

Your earlier note gives the contrast a concrete shape: you spoke quickly and led the meeting, listened more at dinner, and still held the same view about the timetable in both settings. That suggests continuity in your judgment even though your manner changed. Feeling comfortable in both settings also matters: it leaves open the possibility that both voices are genuinely yours, each responsive to a different relationship and situation.

Hume’s *Of personal identity* pushes in a related direction: he argues that what we call the self is not one unchanging impression but a succession of changing perceptions connected in experience ([Hume, “Of personal identity”](https://davidhume.org/texts/t/1/4/6)). Neither Hume nor Carroll proves that your two voices are equally authentic, but they both challenge the demand that authenticity must sound the same everywhere.

A useful question may be less “Which voice is the real me?” and more: **What commitments, values, or ways of relating remain recognizable across both voices—and where, if anywhere, do you feel a tension between them?**

The Caterpillar and Alice looked at each other for some time in
silence: at last the Caterpillar took the hookah out of its mouth, and
addressed her in a languid, sleepy voice.

“Who are _you?_” said the Caterpillar.

This was not an encouraging opening for a conversation. Alice replied,
rather shyly, “I—I hardly know, sir, just at present—at least I know
who I _was_ when I got up this morning, but I think I must have been
changed several times since then.”

“What do you mean by that?” said the Caterpillar sternly. “Explain
yourself!”

“I can’t explain _myself_, I’m afraid, sir,” said Alice, “because I’m
not myself, you see.”

“I don’t see,” said the Caterpillar.

“I’m afraid I can’t put it more clearly,” Alice replied very politely,
“for I can’t understand it myself to begin with; and being so many
different sizes in a day is very confusing.”

“It isn’t,” said the Caterpillar.

“Well, perhaps you haven’t found it so yet,” said Alice; “but when you
have to turn into a chrysalis—you will some day, you know—and then
after that into a butterfly, I should think you’ll feel it a little
queer, won’t you?”

“Not a bit,” said the Caterpillar.

“Well, perhaps your feelings may be different,” said Alice; “all I know
is, it would feel very queer to _me_.”

“You!” said the Caterpillar contemptuously. “Who are _you?_”

Which brought them back again to the beginning of the conversation.
Alice felt a little irritated at the Caterpillar’s making such _very_
short remarks, and she drew herself up and said, very gravely, “I
think, you ought to tell me who _you_ are, first.”

“Why?” said the Caterpillar.

Here was another puzzling question; and as Alice could not think of any
good reason, and as the Caterpillar seemed to be in a _very_ unpleasant
state of mind, she turned away.

“Come back!” the Caterpillar called after her. “I’ve something
important to say!”

This sounded promising, certainly: Alice turned and came back again.

“Keep your temper,” said the Caterpillar.

“Is that all?” said Alice, swallowing down her anger as well as she
could.
